newsitem.headline: Reuters 17th ex-Dubai air cargo market report.

text.p: Below are the current average ex- Dubai air cargo market rates in United Arab Emirates dirhams per kg for a 100 kg shipment, with volume-to-weight ratio of six-to-one:

*The rates quoted in the report were obtained by Reuter journalists on a confidential basis from a range of airlines, large forwarders and smaller air cargo agents.
*The tariffs represent average rates calculated from a range of prices and are indicative of current market activity.
*A UAE dirham is fixed at a rate of $0.27.
Dubai sees first signs of air cargo market recovery
By Hilary Gush

DUBAI, Sept 30 (Reuter) - Air cargo operators in Dubai say they are seeing the first signs of recovery in the market which has for months been languishing in the doldrums, but they say rates are still way off what they see as reasonable levels.
"This year the market has been very, very poor. But recently things are getting better out of Dubai," a cargo manager at a carrier dominant in the ex-Dubai market said.
"Loads are slowly increasing, now we expect to see some rate adjustments," he added.

Airlines and forwarders say volumes are slowly lifting off their rock-bottom summer levels, but this has had no significant impact on rates. Sea-air freight shipments are sharply down on a year ago and airlines are looking more to air-to-air shipments.
"Maybe rates will now turn the corner," said a forwarder.
"Sea-air has really fallen and continues on a declining path because the Far East and subcontinent feed has dried," he added.
Sea-air freight volumes fell a year-on-year 16.4 percent in August to nearly 5,121 tonnes, Dubai Cargo Village figures show.
This is the fifth consecutive fall so far in 1996.
Much of Dubai's position as a trading and re-export hub is based on its location mid-way between East and West and its proximity to the Indian subcontinent.

Goods are brought in bulk by sea and are then broken down into smaller parcels and sent by air, smaller ships and traditional wooden dhows around the world. The air cargo shipments are mainly destined to Europe and the United States.
But lower air freight rates in the Far East and Indian subcontinent this year have prompted shippers to send their goods directly by air, operators say.
"The Far East overflow used to come through us, but now that capacity has been put on directly and shipping lines are faster, Dubai is missing out," said one cargo manager.
But Dubai is still seeing some air-to-air shipments.

"There are a lot of air-to-air shipments, mainly from Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. We are not seeing many from India because shippers there can buy directly to New York more cheaply," another airline cargo manager said.
He said fewer spot rates were being offered on some sectors, so the rate floor had moved up. Spot rates are those offered to shippers in the 24 hours before take-off.
"At one stage some were selling 3.20 (dirhams a kg) to Europe, but now its up at 3.50," he said.

Reuters calculates the average rate on a 100 kg shipment with a six-to-one volume-to-weight ratio to London Heathrow five fils firmer at 3.62 dirhams. Similarly, the average rate to Frankfurt is 3.62 from 3.57 dirhams.

Players said extra flights put on to the Indian subcontinent at the end of September to cope with a flood of passengers taking advantage of a UAE government amnesty on illegal immigrants had affected the market little.

"We are not seeing an impact as many of the amnesty people are carrying a lot of personal effects with them. Also, demand to the Indian subcontinent from Dubai is never very great," the cargo manager at a large European carrier said.
But he said the extra flights offered more capacity out of the subcontinent into Dubai. "There is an opportunity because flights are coming in empty from the subcontinent," he said.
The United Arab Emirates has announced an extension of the September 30 deadline to October 31 for an estimated 200,000 illegal immigrants to legalise their stay or leave.
Thousands of workers, mainly from India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and the Philippines, have been scrambling to leave by air and boat to avoid penalties when the amnesty ends.
An Air India official said his airline had put on an extra 39 flights and re-routed another 14 through the United Arab Emirates since the amnesty was first announced in August.
Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) put on 15 extra flights through Dubai and another 12 through Abu Dhabi and Al Ain in the last two weeks of September.

PIA Dubai manager Zahid Afridi said as cargo capacity through Dubai had been constrained by the amnesty passengers, two extra Boeing 707 freighters, originating in Frankfurt, had flown through Dubai to Lahore in the past two weeks.
To the United States business remains weak. The average rate to JKF in New York is at 5.80 dirhams a kg and the rate to Los Angeles is also unchanged at an average 6.60.
"We can't carry on like this. To the U.S. our prices have dropped 30-40 percent in the past 18 months," an airline representative said.
"We need to sit down and discuss how we can get a few extra cents. Cargo is not making a healthy contribution," he added.
Business to the Far East is on an even keel, with average rates to Singapore and Hong Kong steady at last month's 3.90.
To Nairobi the average rate on a 100 kg shipment is keeping within its established 3.90-3.95 band, at 3.90 dirhams a kg from 3.93.
Players expect business to most stations to improve slowly but surely in the run-up to Christmas and New Year.
"It should get better from now until about December 20 and then things will slow down for New Year holidays, Ramadan and the Chinese New Year," said one.
"1996 has not been an exciting year. We pray that this market will get better," the Dubai cargo manager of a large Asian carrier said.
